newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-FURIOUS ACTION MARKS MAJOR LEAGUE TRADE DEADLINE.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-FURIOUS ACTION MARKS MAJOR LEAGUE TRADE DEADLINE.

text.p: The St. Louis Cardinals acquired Mark McGwire to push for the pennant, the Chicago White Sox waved the white flag and the Seattle Mariners tried to bolster their woeful bullpen in a trade deadline flurry on Thursday.

The Cardinals shipped reliever T.J. Mathews and a pair of minor-league pitchers to the Oakland Athletics to get McGwire, one of the baseball's greatest sluggers. In St. Louis, the 33-year-old McGwire will be reunited with Tony La Russa, who managed him for 10 years with the Athletics.

McGwire, a nine-time All-Star who can be a free agent at the end of the season, is batting .284 with 34 homers and 81 RBI and averaging a home run every 10.8 at-bats this year. His career home run ratio of one every 12.25 at-bats is second only to Babe Ruth's one per 11.76 at-bats. The last four seasons, McGwire's ratio is an astounding one per 9.27.
To get McGwire, St. Louis, who are 7 1/2 games behind the NL Central-leading Houston Astros, also sent right-handers Eric Ludwick and Blake Stein to the Athletics.
The 27-year-old Mathews could assume the closer's role in the Oakland bullpen. He was 4-4 with a 2.15 ERA in 40 relief appearances this year.

The White Sox, just 3 1/2 games behind first-place Cleveland in the AL Central, all but conceded the division by sending ace left-hander Wilson Alvarez, closer Roberto Hernandez and veteran right-hander Danny Darwin to the San Francisco Giants.
In return, Chicago got six minor leaguers. The move came two days after the White Sox traded designated hitter Harold Baines back to the Baltimore Orioles for a player to be named.
Both Alvarez and Hernandez are in the last year of their contracts and can become free agents after this season, but Chicago's drastic divestiture still came as a shock.
Alvarez (9-8) led the club in wins and strikeouts (110) and boasted a 3.03 ERA in 22 starts.
Hernandez, in his seventh year with the White Sox and fifth as their closer, was 5-1 with 27 saves and a 2.44 ERA.

Owner Jerry Reinsdorf hinted at the impending downsizing when he told the Chicago Sun Times on Thursday: "Anyone who thinks this White Sox team will catch Cleveland is crazy. We're not even in second place, so we have to prepare for next year and the future."

The Giants were desperately searching for pitching help to improve a team that has lost 13 of its last 21 games and has fallen into a first-place tie with the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League West.
The players going to Chicago are shortstop Mike Caruso, outfielder Brian Manning and pitchers Lorenzo Barcelo, Keith Foulke, Bob Howry and Ken Vining.

Seattle tried to improve their beleaguered bullpen by swinging a pair of deals, sending highly touted outfielder Jose Cruz Jr. to the Toronto Blue Jays for right-hander Mike Timlin and left-hander Paul Spoljaric.

The Mariners, who lead AL West by a mere half-game over the Anaheim Angels, also picked up inconsistent closer Heathcliff Slocumb from the Boston Red Sox for catching prospect Jason Varitek and pitcher Derek Lowe.

The Cleveland Indians, seeking help for an injury-riddled rotation, acquired veteran left-hander John Smiley in a six-player deal with the Cincinnati Reds, then obtained big right-hander Jeff Juden from the Montreal Expos for lefty Steve Kline.

Smiley is 9-10 with a poor 5.23 ERA, but his last four starts have been impressive. Cleveland also received infielder Jeff Branson, and in return sent pitchers Danny Graves, Scott Winchester and Jim Crowell along with infielder Damian Jackson to the Reds.
One player who did not change addresses was All-Star catcher Ivan Rodriguez, who agreed to a five-year, $42 million deal to stay with the Texas Rangers.
Rodriguez, one of the best all-around catchers in baseball, is hitting .332 with 11 homers and 47 RBI.

The deal, which includes a $1 million signing bonus, will pay "Pudge" $6 million next season, $8 million a year from 1999-2001 and $9 million in 2002. Rodriguez also will receive $2 million in severance pay and he and the club agreed to donate $1 million to two charities.
Teams can still make trades after the deadline, but deals then have to go through waivers, which complicates the process and allows competitors to void them by making waiver claims.
